To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Oruanui super-eruption occurred in two phases: a prelude of ~1.5 kyr of mafic eruptions, followed by a 2-day rhyolitic eruption.

the 25.7 ka Oruanii supereruption was triggered by a combination of tectonic processes and magmatic overpressure, and that the eruption was a complex, episodic event that involved the assembly and eruption (in 1 day) of a super-sized crystal-poor rholite magma body, which was generated from an underlying crystal-rich magma mush.

(1) The 530 km ^{3} Oruanui rhyolite magma was generated over tens of thousands of years by fractional crystallisation of an andesite magma, and assembled into an eruptible body over a few hundred years; (2) The Oruanui magma was assembled from a crystal-rich (melt-poor) mush body, which was generated by fractional crystallisation, and a low-silica melt-dominant magma that was generated by partial melting
In summary, our research is concerned with

the processes that drive the generation and accumulation of large volumes of crystal-poor magma, the processes that control the evolution of this magma, and the processes that control its release episodicity.
the processes that lead to the formation of large-volume eruptions and the implications this has on volcanic hazards.
the generation, accumulation, and eruption of the largest rhyolitic eruption on Earth during the Holocene.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Oruanui super-eruption occurred in two stages, the second of which was triggered by tectonic stresses.
the Oruanui super eruption is a textbook example of how a super-sized magma system can be assembled and erupted in a geologically rapid timeframe.
the Oruanui eruption was a super-sized, multi-phase, multi-component, magmatic event.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Oruanui super-eruption was the result of a cascade of magmatic processes that were triggered and controlled by external forces.
the Oruanui eruption was not triggered by the mafic magma, but was instead a result of a long-term accumulation of magma, which eventually exceeded the strength of the overlying crust.
the Oruanui eruption was a cascade of magmatic processes that began tens of thousands of years before the eruption and continued for months after the eruption ended.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the eruption was triggered by the arrival of a large volume of low-silica, hot rhyolite magma at the base of the eruptible magma chamber, which rapidly cooled to eruptible temperatures, and was subsequently erupted.

a super-sized eruptible magma body can be assembled and evacuated in a relatively short time frame, in a matter of decades, by a cascade of magmatic processes that are not necessarily related to each other.
the Oruanui eruption was a complex, multi-phase, super-eruption, driven by a series of magmatic events, which were themselves controlled by the tectonic environment.
